newsitem.title: CANADA: Noranda focuses on metals for 1997 growth.
newsitem.headline: Noranda focuses on metals for 1997 growth.

text.p: Noranda Inc plans to focus on its mining and metallurgy sector for growth in 1997, the company's chief financial officer Alan Thomas said on Thursday.
"We think that's where the best opportunities are at this point," Thomas said in a phone interview.

The company is placing its hopes for growth mainly in the Falconbridge Ltd's Raglan nickel project in Quebec, which is expected to start production in late 1997, Thomas said. Noranda owns 46.3 percent of Falconbridge.
But zinc production for 1997 is expected to fall slightly.
The company produced 494,000 tonnes of zinc in 1996, compared to 565,000 tonnes in 1995. Zinc production is expected to be about five percent lower in 1997, Thomas said.
At the company's Brunswich zinc mine, Noranda expects to produce about 9,000 tonnes of ore per day, a 10 percent decrease from last year's planned rate of production.
Noranda cut back production to about 8,500 tonnes a day from an average 9,600 tonnes a day last summer for safety reasons.
"I think we have a mining plan that will put us right back on track," Thomas said..
The company also plans some small expansions in its metallurgy operations, Thomas said.
"There are a number projects that are incremental expansions -- two, three, four or five percent. It's not major but it's very important," he said.

But Noranda does not foresee much growth in its forestry or oil and gas sectors. The company plans to add a new oriented strand board plant in 1998, but for 1997 the company expects a short-term oversupply of the wood product, Thomas said.
The company is exploring for growth in oil and gas.
But growth through acquisition in the oil and gas area is too expensive to be considered right now, Thomas said.
Acquisition in the mining sector, however, is high on Noranda's list of priorities.
"We're looking at a number of opportunities whcih could have substantial impact, but they're only at the early stages," he said, without giving details.
He said the company was searching worldwide, but was not concentrating on any particular metal.
"We like them all. We'll take anything," he said.
The company is also placing a lot of faith in magnesium.
Noranda poured its first magnesium last Friday at a pilot project in Quebec using a new process it designed, Thomas said.
The company will decide this spring whether it will build a C$500 million refinery to take the project full scale, he added. The refinery would take three years to build.
Feed would come from tailings of old asbestos mines in Quebec.
"The raw material is just waiting to be taken," said Thomas. "It looks terrific (so far). We poured our first metal last Friday and proved it works."
The project, of which Noranda controls more than 50 percent, would account for about 20 percent of the world's magnesium supply, he said.
"It probably has the greatest outlook at this point," he explained. "Because of its weight to strength ratio, it's much lighter than aluminum or steel. There are tremendous growth opportunities."
((Heather Scoffield, Reuters Toronto Bureau 416 941-8104))
